title: Humanity Is Plagued By The Open Loop
body: We're obsessed with closing loops. Say goodbye before someone dies. Get the last word in an argument. Finish the project instead of shelving it. Get an answer, any answer, instead of sitting with "I don't know."

Here's the uncomfortable part: a lot of the time, the other side of that loop doesn't even know it's open. If someone dies before you get to say goodbye, they don't experience an incomplete goodbye. There's no ledger on their end waiting to be balanced. The open loop was always yours. You weren't closing something for them. You were closing something in your own head.

An open loop is really just an unanswered question about your own footing — did I handle that, is this going to come back on me. Not-knowing feels like exposure. Closing the loop, even badly, turns an unknown into a known. That's why you re-send an email you already sent, or over-explain a decision that was already fine — nothing about the outcome changes, but the exposure does.

Here's the trap: your brain can't tell the difference between a loop that's resolved and one that's resolved well. It only tracks open versus closed. A trivial unanswered text costs the same anxious energy as a genuinely important unfinished project, because to your nervous system, both just register as "open." Your task list works the same way. Half of what's on it isn't urgent, it's just open — and open is uncomfortable enough that you'll work on the wrong thing just to make a loop disappear.
So the fix isn't "finish more things." It's closing loops on purpose, cheaply, when the work wouldn't have mattered anyway:

list: Write the "no" down. A task you've quietly already decided not to do stays open forever if you never officially closed it. Cross it off. A decided "no" is an ending, same as a finished "yes" — and if it was actually important, it'll raise its head again on its own. You don't need to keep it open just in case; the ones that matter come back without your help.

Separate the list from the priority. Write down everything, then star the few that actually matter. That's it. The starred items get your attention. Everything else can sit on the list unstarred and stop competing for the same anxiety.

Notice the loops that were never yours to close. Some open loops are you chasing someone else's reaction or peace of mind. You don't control that ending. Naming it as not yours is sometimes the only close available.

body: Not every open loop deserves to be closed well. Some just need an ending — any ending — so your head can stop paying rent on something that was never going to pay you back.
